O.outcome_detail: comfort with collaborative active learning and perceived control over teamwork

cells.quote: In our interviews, a common coping method that came up with participants was self-assignment to the same types of roles when working in teams. Some of our participants (P2, P3, P4) said that they often took on more clerical or managerial roles, describing how it allowed them to have more control over the way work was conducted, structured, and formatted.
cells.note: The interview evidence describes self-assigned roles as a coping method that increased perceived control and helped participants manage collaborative work; it does not report a formal quantitative comparison or effect size.

D.treatment: explicitly stating access needs to teammates

O.outcome_detail: comfort and participation in collaborative active learning

cells.quote: P2 went on to describe how this can cause conflict within their groups, especially when their teammates do not understand why they may need a more structured approach to collaborative work. They found that being very explicit with their access needs [20] (i.e., the things people need to fully participate in a space or activity) was helpful, stating, “​​[Other students] don’t really know that I struggle with some things, they would consider me as just another person who is neurotypical, and they wouldn’t really know that I have some expectations.”
cells.note: The comparison is implicit: explicit access-needs communication versus leaving needs uncommunicated. The qualitative finding reports that explicit communication was helpful, without a quantified effect or specified timing.
